Items.Authors: Tom van der Wielen, Elmar Schmälzlin, Martin Roth
Items.Title: Using an integral field unit for multiplexed confocal Raman microscopy
Items.Abstract: MUSE-Transfer is a technology transfer project that aims to use an integral field unit (IFU) for confocal Raman microscopy. Raman spectrometers analyze the back scattered light of a laser beam interacting with a material, providing a unique molecular fingerprint. Applications are quality control in the semiconductor industry, medicine and drug discovery.    Raman signals are faint, which makes creating chemical maps time-consuming. State of the art scanning techniques manage to capture a spectrum every millisecond, which still leads to large acquisition times at scale (megapixels). Our previous publications employ the multi-channel optical trains of MUSE and VIRUS for Raman setups and demonstrated that 2D Raman images for identifying skin tumors can be recorded within 2 minutes.    The current challenge is to address 3D Raman measurements. To facilitate z-scanning, we use a confocal optical train, which filters lights not strictly from the focal plane, and bi-telecentric optics.

Items.Authors: Sergey Sichevsky, Vladimir Shmagin, Mikhail Sachkov, Evgeniy A. Kopylov
Items.Title: UV detectors of the Spektr-UF mission
Items.Abstract: The key task of the Spektr-UV orbital observatory is to conduct astrophysical observations in the ultraviolet wavelength range (115-310 nm), inaccessible to ground-based instruments. The registration of radiation in this range in the Field Camera Unit is assigned to a bundle of an electron-optical converter and a high-speed reader with specific mission requirements in terms of frame rate, algorithms for processing data in the mode of recording individual photons, radiation resistance and reliability in space flight. In this paper, we present a description of the architecture of a specialized radiation receiver unit, including a photodetector based on a CMOS sensor and a control electronics unit designed to solve scientific problems at the Spektr-UV observatory, in particular, for high-speed reading and processing of data from an electron-optical converter. Successful The implementation of the detector will ensure the fulfillment of one of the main scientific functions of the Spektr-UV

Items.Authors: Tilo Steinmetz, Yuanjie Wu, Ronald Holzwarth, Alexander Jakob, Karsten Winkler, Hanna Kellermann, Frank Grupp
Items.Title: UV extension of astrocombs
Items.Abstract: We present a broadband, spectrally flattened astrocomb for calibrating astronomical spectrographs across the U- to K-band. We extend our standard visible to near-infrared AstroComb into the UV using an achromatic second-harmonic generation (aSHG) stage with optimized focusing for broadband and spectrally flat conversion. This approach minimizes UV load on sensitive optics, improving long-term stability. Initial tests at the FOCES spectrograph (Mount Wendelstein Observatory) with a 25 GHz mode spacing demonstrate uniform spectral output, high line contrast, and dense calibration lines from the near-UV through the visible. With this work, we demonstrate the long-anticipated extension of the astrocomb technology into the UV, enabling full U- to K-band spectrograph calibration capability.

Items.Authors: Andrea Bianco, Claudia Brambilla, Michele Frangiamore, Davide Giughello, Dirhaj Gupta
Items.Title: VPHG@INAF: results and perspective for spectrographs from UV to IR
Items.Abstract: Volume Phase Holographic (VPH) technology is extremely important in modern, mainly groud-based, astronomical spectrographs thanks to some quite unique features, such as: high diffraction efficiency, wide tunability, robustness. At the INAF-Astronomical Observatory of Brera we have been working on the design and manufacturing of VPHGs for different instrumentation in the spectral range from 350nm and 2500nm. In this paper, we report the recent results we had on VPHGs in terms of diffraction efficiency, wavefront error and overall optical quality highlighting the improvement we have had since the last SPIE. Moreover, we provide an outlook of the performances we expect in the next years.

Items.Authors: Simone Di Filippo, Gabriele Umbriaco, Jacopo Farinato, Demetrio Magrin, Mirko Colapietro, Salvatore Savarese, Pietro Schipani, Sergio D'Orsi, Laurent Marty, Giulio Capasso, Francesco Perrotta, Stefano Covino, Silvio Di Rosa
Items.Title: VSTPOL: the commissioning plan
Items.Abstract: VSTPOL is a polarimetric module upgrading the 2.6-m VLT Survey Telescope (VST) for wide-field optical imaging polarimetry, making it the first large survey telescope capable of linear polarimetry. It supports key science, including optical follow-up of sources from the co-located Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). VSTPOL replaces the existing opto-mechanical assembly between the primary mirror cell and OmegaCAM with a redesigned unit, combining two plano-spherical lenses and a linear polarizer, operated via synchronized linear and rotational stages for filter insertion, polarization-angle setting, and continuous field-rotation compensation. This paper presents the Assembly, Integration, and Verification plan for installation and commissioning at Paranal, covering removal of the old system, verification, optical alignment, and final re-installation. Completion is expected by the end of 2026.

Items.Authors: Christian Schwab, Ron Appels, Julien Storm, Jacob Pember, Gert Raskin, Rik ter Horst, Ronnie Appels, Nick Binos
Items.Title: Wavefront corrections of large cross-disperser prisms for echelle spectrometers
Items.Abstract: Prisms are attractive cross-dispersers for high-resolution echelle spectrometers because they span more than an octave with high throughput and no light lost to unwanted diffraction orders. For large astronomical Echelles, however, obtaining optical glass with sufficient transmission, dispersion, and quality to accommodate ~200 mm beams is a major challenge. A 60° F2-type prism with a 200 mm projected aperture is over 340 mm long, and even small index inhomogeneities across this distance can produce transmitted wavefront errors that degrade resolution and increase crosstalk.   We faced these issues in the MARVEL and Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT) spectrometers, both of which use large F2 prisms that required manual wavefront correction to meet performance goals. We describe the correction process and present the resulting improvements in transmitted wavefront error, point-spread function, and measured birefringence.

Items.Authors: Gerardo Avila Soberanes, Carlos Guirao, Roman Guemperlein
Items.Title: WHAPOS: a high efficiency medium resolution fiber-fed spectrograph
Items.Abstract: WHAPOS is a compact, fiber-fed spectrograph with a resolving power of 24,000, developed by Baader Planetarium in Germany. The instrument's design optimizes throughput along the 392-750 nm spectral range. The instrument's peak order efficiency is greater than 35% for wavelengths greater than 450 nm, excluding the detector quantum efficiency but including the fiber link. The optics are mounted on a carbon fiber-reinforced polymer table for maximum mechanical and thermal stability. The spectrograph is mounted in a double enclosure that includes an active thermal control system. The spectrograph temperature is maintained within variations of less than 0.1°C by this system.    WHAPOS is optimized for small and medium telescopes. It has been successfully tested in the 1-meter telescope at the VEGA Observatory and the 1.5-meter telescope at the Sierra Nevada Observatory. In this paper, we present the design, performance, and preliminary astronomical results of WHAPOS.

Items.Authors: Paul J. Kuzmenko, Morgan T. Burks, Nathan R. Hines
Items.Title: What's old is new again: an activated charcoal cryosorption pump for the Dragonfly gamma ray spectrometer
Items.Abstract: The gamma ray spectrometer on NASA’s Dragonfly mission requires good vacuum  insulation so that its germanium element can be annealed in Titan’s 94 K  environment without drawing excessive electrical power. After rejecting several  concepts that could not meet size, weight, and power requirements we chose an  activated charcoal cryosorption pump. Its performance was verified by laboratory  testing.

Items.Authors: Benoit Sassolas, Matthieu Coulon, Christophe Michel, Laurent Pinard, Roland Bacon, Corentin Cudennec, Philippe Dierickx
Items.Title: Widefield Spectroscopic Telescope (WST): coating strategy to achieve high optical throughput
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a 12-m class facility designed for simultaneous wide-field multi-object and integral-field spectroscopy across 370–1600 nm, targeting a throughput above 83% its wide-field focus and 0.76 at its integral field one. Its 13 mirrors and 5 lenses require optimised coatings balancing feasibility, operational needs, and long-term durability. Large mirrors (>2 m) may use enhanced metallic coatings, such as the protected-silver solution from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, achieving over 90% reflectivity in UV and above 99% in NIR. Smaller mirrors would use Nb₂O₅/SiO₂ dielectric stacks, offering ~99% reflectivity, tunable spectral response, and excellent stability. Coating the large lenses (up to 1.6 m) is challenging due to the ultra-broadband range; traditional multilayer antireflective coatings show limitations from manufacturing and incidence-angle effects. Graded-index AR coatings are being explored for superior performance.

Items.Authors: Sébastien Pernecker, Maxime Rombach, Roelof de Jong, Aaron Omadutt, Younes Chahid, Anmol Goyal, David Lee, Joseph W. Barrow, Jean-Paul Kneib, Oliver Pineda Suárez, Malak Galal, Will Saunders, Chris Waring, Jonathan Wei
Items.Title: WST multi-object spectrograph fiber positioners: development of a 32,000-unit precision robotic system
Items.Abstract: The Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope Multi-Object Spectrograph requires an unprecedented fiber positioning  system comprising 30,000 low-resolution and 2,000 high-resolution positioners across a 3.1 deg² field of view.  Each robotic positioner must achieve 5 μm RMS positioning accuracy in a densely packed focal plane. To mitigate risks  associated with industrial-scale production of 32,000 precision mechanisms, WST is pursuing a multi-concept  development strategy. Four distinct positioner architectures are being prototyped and tested by an interna-  tional collaboration (EPFL, AIP, UKATC, AAO) using 6.2 mm pitch triangular modules of 63 units each or a  new inline modular concept. Performance metrics including positioning accuracy, repeatability, reconfiguration  speed, collision avoidance, and manufacturability are being systematically evaluated. Down-selection to one or  two concepts is planned for 2026-2027.

Items.Authors: Simone D'Auria, Vincenzo Cianniello, Ciro Del Vecchio, Vincenzo De Caprio, Philippe Dierickx, Gaston Gausachs, Tony Trauvillon, William Sutherland, Olga Bellido
Items.Title: WST, the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope: telescope structure FE analyses
Items.Abstract: The altitude structure of the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope(WST) supports the primary and secondary mirrors and represents one of the main structural subsystems of the telescope. Owing to its size and mass, its static and dynamic behavior directly affects telescope performance. This work presents a preliminary structural assessment based on a finite element model developed from the conceptual design. The structure was modeled using beam and shell elements under representative boundary conditions to reproduce the operational environment. The analyses provided estimates of structural mass, stress distribution, deformations, and natural frequencies, enabling the identification of the most relevant global vibration modes. Based on the obtained results, a preliminary optimization study was carried out by varying selected beam cross-sections and shell thicknesses. The study led to an improved structural configuration and provided the basis for the definition of the main design criteria.

Items.Authors: Mansi M. Kasliwal
Items.Title: Unveiling our dynamic infrared sky with Roman RAPID and Cryoscope
Items.Abstract: Many astronomical events shine the brightest in the infrared (IR) due to atomic opacity, self enshrouding, dust extinction, or low temperature. When we saw the first electromagnetic counterpart to gravitational waves from a neutron star merger, it was the rapid reddening and IR spectral features that confirmed the synthesis of heavy elements by the r-process. Neutron star black hole mergers may shine brightest in the IR. Stellar mergers, planet-star engulfments and mass-losing stars are also extremely red due to self obscuration. Yet, the IR time-domain is hitherto largely unexplored. In this talk, I will present a status update on the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope that is scheduled to launch in Fall 2026. I will describe RAPID (Roman Alerts Promptly from Image Differencing); a Project Infrastructure Team committed to enabling time-domain astronomy with Roman. I will conclude with plans for an IR dream machine that leverages two breakthrough technologies: Cryoscope in Antarctica.

Items.Authors: John L. Jørgensen
Items.Title: PIXL, the Perseverance autonomous XRF instrument suite
Items.Abstract: PIXL, the Perseverance autonomous X-Ray fluorescence microscope, is optimized to perform mineralogy of rocks down to the grain size, including compositions and morphology. Mounted on the boom-tip of the robotic arm, operating in unknown terrain, at rough surfaces, the instrument is highly autonomous. One of the key tasks of Perseverance, to detect and map areas of potential habitability of the Martian distant past, necessitated a specialized instrument portfolio. Another objective is to constraint the evolution path from an ancient wet mild climate to the present-day desert planet conditions. PIXL is the first instrument of its class to Mars, and have made several surprising observations, from igneous rock formation to reaction fronts closely resembling Earthly formations altered by paleo-bacterial life. We present the PIXL instrument, the optimizations made and the autonomy realized, and present some of the important observations.

Items.Authors: P. Chris Broekema
Items.Title: Affordable and sustainable large-scale distributed radio telescope processing
Items.Abstract: Producing science-ready data products from large-scale radio  telescopes is computationally, financially and environmentally  expensive. In light of the current climate crisis, we can no longer  accept that improving scientific instruments inevitably results in an  unconstrained increase in processing requirements. Starting this year,  ASTRON aims to increase the capabilities of the international LOFAR  telescope, within the current energy budget. In this talk we will  highlight some of envisioned challenge and we will discuss in some  detail the efforts to achieve this ambitious goal. We will take a look  at the technologies used to improve efficiency and measure the  environmental impact of various operations in the signal processing  pipeline. A key component of this is operator and end-user  awareness. We will close with an outlook at the applicability of  emerging and future technologies and their impact on environmental  impact.

Items.Authors: Philip M. Hinz, Antonin Bouchez, Richard Dekany, Jessica R. Lu, Mark Chun, Daren Dillon, Jason Fucik, Prakriti Gupta, Brad Holden, Aaron Hunter, Marc Kassis, Matias Kidron, Stefan Kuiper, Renate Kupke, Matt Maniscalco, Nick MacDonald, Eduardo Marin, Reston Nash, Emily Plume, Matthew Radovan, Chris Ratliff, Mitsuko Roberts, Roger Smith, R. Deno Stelter, Jacob Taylor
Items.Title: An integrated adaptive optics facility for the Keck 1 Telescope
Items.Abstract: Adaptive optics that is integrated into the telescope provides greater transmission, lower emissivity, higher contrast, and higher sky coverage compared to post-focal plane systems. It enables a broader range of correction capabilities, including ground-layer and multiconjugate correction. Based on a new adaptive secondary mirror for Keck 1, we are developing a comprehensive system for image quality enhancement across the full instrument suite.  This paper describes the science case, system requirements, and testing plans for the new Keck-1 Adaptive Optics Facility. The facility will: 1) improve image quality for wide-field spectrometers, 2) enhance performance and throughput for diffraction-limited instruments, and 3) improve sensitivity for time-domain instruments. The facility will support future multiconjugate and high-contrast AO capabilities.  We describe the adaptive secondary mirror, wavefront sensing, laser beacon systems, realtime computer suite, and commissioning approach.

Items.Authors: Stefano Di Frischia, Gianluca Marotta, Elisabetta Giani, Carlo Baffa, Ivana Novak, Martino Colciago, Bruno Coelho, Matteo Canzari, Matteo Di Carlo
Items.Title: Anomaly detection in SKA monitor and control data using deep learning models
Items.Abstract: In the complex and distributed environment of SKA Observatory, predictive maintenance will play a crucial role, aiming to forecast failures and malfunctions by analyzing data to identify early warning signs. Anomaly detection acts as the core engine for this process, identifying unusual patterns or deviations from normal operating. Within this context, lacking years of historical production data, a large amount of CSP (Central SIgnal Processor) monitor and control data are being collected during ci/cd pipeline jobs.   The data generated during these tests is invaluable for establishing a valid operational baseline.Therefore a range of deep learning models are trained to recognize the normal operational baseline of the observatory's equipment. Once this baseline is established, the system can identify any data points or patterns that deviate significantly from the standard.   The results of such AI-models are then summarized and compared following standard benchmark metrics of classifier

Items.Authors: Michael W. McElwain, Jane Rigby, Marshall D. Perrin, Lee D. Feinberg, Julie M. Van Campen, Knicole Colon, Stefanie N. Milam, Matthew D. Lallo
Items.Title: JWST at four years: prime mission highlights and legacy
Items.Abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has achieved spectacular success as an infrared space observatory, marking a new era in astrophysics and planetary science. JWST developed many new technologies and was the first to demonstrate segmented-telescope wavefront sensing in space, providing a path to even larger space telescopes. The observatory's performance has exceeded expectations, delivering unprecedented infrared sensitivity. The science mission has transformed our understanding of the early universe, exoplanet atmospheres, stellar formation, and galaxy evolution. The lessons learned from its design, deployment, and operations provide key insights for the development and implementation of next-generation space telescopes and astronomical instrumentation. This presentation will report on the JWST prime mission highlights and its lasting legacy for space science.

Items.Authors: Cyril Petit, Stéphane Basa, Romain Fétick, Yves-Michel Frédéric, Gillian Leplat, Pierre-Louis Mayeur, Jean-Francois Sauvage, Ugo Tricoli, Pierre Vernazza, Nicolas Védrenne, Thierry Fusco
Items.Title: Onera’s 2.5 m class telescope for space domain awareness ‘PROVIDENCE’: scientific roadmap and programmatic strategy
Items.Abstract: Space Domain Awareness (SDA) is crucial for defense and civilian use. Ground based high resolution imaging with large telescopes and adaptive optics can deliver detailed image sequences of resident space objects (RSO), complemented by additional signatures for characterization. ONERA, together with CNRS/OSU Pythéas, is developing the PROVIDENCE project, a 2.5 m telescope optimized for SDA, equipped with adaptive optics, spectro imagers and advanced post processing. Installed at the Observatoire de Haute Provence, first light is planned for 2028, making it Europe’s unique research platform for space observation, covering LEO and GEO monitoring, astrophysics, quantum communications, solar system studies, and transient astronomy. We shall describe the scientific roadmap, the programmatic strategy including development of related tools, prototyping actions and some preliminary results.

Items.Authors: Guilhem Terrasa, Aline Hermans, Ann Baeke, Alexandra Mazzoli, Rik Huygen, Sara Regibo, Pierre Royer, Bart Vandenbussche
Items.Title: PLATO cameras alignment, assembly and post-test verification
Items.Abstract: PLATO is an exoplanet hunting mission of the European Space Agency. It is a medium-class mission, with a launch foreseen in 2027 with the prime objective of uncovering Earth-sized planets residing in their habitable zone. The payload consists of 26 cameras with a very wide field of view aligned at ambient and characterized at cold operational temperature.   In this contribution, we report on the alignment and bolting at ambient of the cameras of Plato, i.e., the input metrology, the mechanical alignment of the optical unit with the focal plane array, and the final fixation of these units. We will also report how the cryo-vacuum performance tests have demonstrated the optical performance of all cameras at operational temperature and confirmed the successfulness of the alignment process performed at ambient.

Items.Authors: Mark Barnet, Suresh Sivanandam, Scott Christie
Items.Title: Quantitative risk analysis on a shoestring: turning risk management into action for small astronomy projects
Items.Abstract: Mid-sized astronomy projects must manage risk without the resources of large programs, often reducing risk management to a paperwork exercise. The Gemini InfraRed Multi-Object Spectrograph (GIRMOS, ~$50M) team developed a lightweight quantitative risk analysis (QRA) framework using a spreadsheet adapted from a Washington State DOT model. The tool uses Monte Carlo simulation to translate qualitative likelihoods and impacts into quantitative estimates of cost and schedule exposure, producing confidence-based contingency budgets and pre-/post-mitigation comparisons. Applied during GIRMOS’s Critical Design Review, the method provided a defensible basis for contingency and schedule planning, transforming risk tracking into an active management process. This “QRA on a shoestring” approach offers mid-sized projects a transparent, data-driven alternative to factored risk tables and percentage-based contingencies.

Items.Authors: Genoveva Micheva, Roelof de Jong, Joar Brynnel, Olga Bellido-Tirado, Marica Valentini, Jakob Walcher
Items.Title: Shift happens - a structured approach to human readiness for the 60 day 4MOST commissioning
Items.Abstract: The 60-day continuous on-sky commissioning of 4MOST required more than technical readiness. It demanded a carefully crafted strategy to prepare a diverse, international, volunteer-based team for a long and sustained operational campaign. Over the course of the last 2.5 years, we implemented a structured training program for the commissioning team, including regular coordination meetings, immersive bootcamps, collaborative coding periods, and focused operational exercises, to build competence, confidence, and shared situational awareness across the team of PhD students, postdocs, and professors. We present the preparation framework and lessons learned, showing how psychological framing, structured training, and distributed responsibility can elevate a volunteer community to high operational readiness for major facility commissioning.

Items.Authors: Frank Eisenhauer, GRAVITY+ Collaboration
Items.Title: The new era of interferometry: where we are and where to go
Items.Abstract: The implementation of laser guide stars on all 8m telescopes of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer marks the beginning of yet another new era of stellar interferometry. Together with new adaptive optics, large-separation fringe tracking, and performance upgrades to the instruments and infrastructure, GRAVITY+ has now opened up the extragalactic sky for milli-arcsecond resolution imaging and provides ever higher contrast for the observation of exoplanets. Following a period of spectacular breakthroughs in selected research areas, including the Galactic Center, the VLTI now serves a wide variety of astrophysics, e.g. star- and planetformation, exoplanets, stellar physics, lensed objects, compact objects, black holes, and extragalactic astrophysics out to cosmological distances. This presentation gives an overview of the current state of interferometry and its results, describes its limitations, discusses the parameter space, and outlines future developments.

Items.Authors: Etienne Pointecouteau, Didier Barret
Items.Title: The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on board newAthena
Items.Abstract: The Advanced Telescope for High Energy Astrophysics (newAthena) is the third large-class mission of the European Space Agency’s Cosmic Vision science program. Designed to explore the Hot and Energetic Universe, newAthena will feature a large-aperture X-ray telescope and two complementary focal plane instruments: the Wide Field Imager (WFI) and the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU). In this paper, I will report on the status of the X-IFU, emphasizing on its anticipated scientific performance, as we prepare the adoption of the mission in early 2027.

Items.Authors: Roland M. Bacon
Items.Title: WST: the next leap in wide-field spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: The WST project aims to design and construct an innovative 10-metre class wide-field spectroscopic survey telescope (WST) in the southern hemisphere. It will feature the parallel operation of two cutting-edge instruments: a high-multiplex (30,000 ), large field-of-view (3 square degrees) multi-object spectrograph (MOS) operating in both low- and high-resolution modes, and a giant panoramic integral field spectrograph (IFS) . WST’s ambitious top-level requirements place it well ahead of all existing and planned spectroscopic facilities. WST capabilities will enable transformative science across a wide range of astrophysical domains. WST is envisioned as the next major facility for ESO following the ELT, and a proposal will be submitted to the ESO Expanding Horizons initiative in 2027.

Items.Authors: Konstantin Waltenberger, Andreas Sinn, Georg Schitter
Items.Title: Daylight pointing calibration for optical telescope systems
Items.Abstract: In daytime operation of optical telescope systems, severe perturbations are introduced, which degrade  optical alignment, pointing precision and imaging quality. This paper describes the development of a single-star-  centering algorithm for robust re-calibration of a telescope pointing model in daylight conditions. The  proposed algorithm and imaging setup results in a 4.1” RMS pointing error for an 80-cm AltAz-telescope.

Items.Authors: Yosuke Minowa, Masayuki Akiyama, Takamasa Bando, Joshua Carter, David Chandler, Richard C.Y. Chou, Jesse Cranney, Céline d'Orgeville, Yutaka Hayano, Dionne Haynes, Roger Haynes, Joschua Hellemeier, Nicholas Herrald, Masayuki Hirabayashi, Yusei Koyama, Andrew Kruse, Noelia Martínez Rey, Masaki Morita, Yuki Moritani, Yoshiyuki Obuchi, Hajime Ogane, Hirofumi Okita, Yoshito Ono, Shin Oya, Naohisa Sato, Yuhei Takagi, Yoko Tanaka, Koki Terao, Chihiro Tokoku, Fumihiro Uraguchi, Lu Wang, Shiang-Yu Wang, Po-Chieh Yu, Michitoshi Yoshida
Items.Title: Final design of ULTIMATE-Subaru ground layer adaptive optics system
Items.Abstract: ULTIMATE-Subaru is the next-generation facility instrument program of the Subaru Telescope, designed to extend the existing Subaru’s wide-field survey capability to the near-infrared (NIR) wavelength. This project includes a Ground-Layer Adaptive Optics (GLAO) and wide-field near-infrared instruments. The main goal of the project is to provide an image size of ~ 0.2 arcsec image size at K band (2.2 micron) across a 20 arcmin diameter field of view at the Cassegrain focus. The GLAO system is scheduled to complete prototyping and final design of its major subsystems by the end of March 2026, subsequently transitioning into the production phase. This presentation will provide an overview of the project, present the results from the prototype tests of the main subsystems, and introduce the final design of the GLAO system. Furthermore, the plan for the manufacturing, assembly, integration, and testing of the GLAO system will be presented.

Items.Authors: Achrene Dyrek, John Stansberry, Bryan Hilbert, Alicia Canipe, Brian Brooks, Martha Boyer, Anton Koekemoer, Everett Schlawin, Nestor Espinoza, Munazza Alam, Julien Girard, Aarynn Carter
Items.Title: Breaking the brightness barrier: JWST/NIRCam DHS spectroscopy for high-precision time-series observations
Items.Abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) offers unprecedented near-infrared sensitivity and stability, enabling time-series observations (TSO) of bright targets. The NIRCam Dispersed Hartmann Sensor (DHS) introduces a new short-wavelength spectroscopic mode, producing up to 8 spatially-separated spectra per source at R~300, and extending coverage down to 1 μm. This new mode will enable spectroscopy of targets as bright as magnitude 3, opening access to high precision studies of bright stars, transiting exoplanets, and any variable high-flux sources. Up-coming calibration efforts will establish flux and wavelength solutions, evaluate saturation and sensitivity limits in combination with the long-wavelength channels (2.4-5 μm), and define optimal procedures for TSO. This presentation will summarize instrument performance, expected calibration results, and guidelines to help the community exploit this new DHS mode for bright-target time-series spectroscopy, once integrated on-board NIRCam.

Items.Authors: Jean Le Graët, Thibault Pichon, Olivier Boulade, Vincent Affato, Frederic Lemmel, Eloy Hernandez, Marion Baumann, Christian Ketchazo, Vincent Moreau, François Visticot
Items.Title: Characterization of IBEX LmAPD detectors at CEA for future low-noise NIR astronomy instruments
Items.Abstract: The next generation of NIR astronomy requires detectors with effective read noise below 1 e⁻. To address this, ESA and Leonardo UK are developing IBEX, a 2k×2k HgCdTe linear-mode APD array with 16 outputs and a 2.5 µm cutoff in avalanche mode. ESA and the Astrophysics Department of CEA are conducting a characterization program on dedicated CEA benches previously used for other NIR detectors, including the ALFA array for the CAGIRE camera. We present first results on one IBEX device, focusing on dark current, effective read noise and effective quantum efficiency as a function of avalanche bias, together with an analysis of non-linearity, crosstalk and persistence in conditions representative of low-noise NIR astronomy.

Items.Authors: Emanuela Orru, Michiel Brentjens, Roberto Francesco Pizzo, Ilse van Bemmel, Cees Bassa, Marco Iacobelli, Vlad Kondratiev, Bernard Asabere, Timothy Shimwell
Items.Title: Commissioning LOFAR 2.0: first results and future plans.
Items.Abstract: LOFAR 2.0 promises to maintain its uniqueness in providing very low frequency high resolution images in the SKA era.  Given the breath of observing modes and functionalities offered by LOFAR 2.0 and expansion towards a fully operational science data center, commissioning is taking place simultaneously to continuous integration and development.  In this talk I will describe the organization and structure of the LOFAR 2.0 commissioning and how the increased complexity of the Array released are taken along with the evolution of the commissioning tests. The same level of attention is given to telescope functionalities, data processing and end to end operations; all these aspects will be discussed in this talk. The state of the art of the system together with initial results and first light images will be shown.

Items.Authors: Etienne Bonnassieux, Damien Gratadour, Marwane Dalal, Cyril Tasse, Arnaud Collioud
Items.Title: Data formats for exascale pipelines with the SKA
Items.Abstract: The upcoming generation of radio interferometers are at the limits of existing data reduction and imaging software capabilities. To address this, a broad collaboration has expanded the widefield direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline used to reduce LoTSS, optimising for deployment on massively distributed architectures, including GPU acceleration. Within ODISSEE, I worked on data format choices to optimise the orchestration and data dispatch, to optimise subsequent reduction on flexible architectures.

Items.Authors: Pavan Bilgi, Guillaume Huber, Michael Bottom, Shane Jacobson, Charles-Antoine Claveau, Markus Loose, Ian M. Baker, Matthew Hicks, Dan Owton, Vincent Isgar, Jordan Ash, Tracy Rook, Anton Lindley-DeCaire
Items.Title: First characterization results of HgCdTe linear mode avalanche photodiodes in a mobile testbed for ultra-low background astronomy.
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) demands IR detectors with sub-electron read noise and dark current < 1 e/px/ks—metrics beyond standard HAWAII-XRG arrays. Linear mode avalanche photodiodes (LmAPDs) stand out as being able to deliver on these requirements while already being compatible with JWST thermal and readout electronics heritage, ensuring HWO readiness. Here, we present the latest on LmAPD development from the University of Hawaii.     Recent tests of "science-grade" devices show < 0.1 e-/px/ks dark current, negligible glow (~0.012 e-/fr), and 0.3 e- rms noise, enabling photon number resolving. To advance to TRL 5, we detail a new mobile cryostat for high-precision QE and radiation testing. We present cryostat vacuum and thermal benchmarks and details of the sensor integration. On sensor characterization progress, we show novel statistical methods for characterizing excess noise factor and gain by analyzing discrete single-photon jumps in non-destructive up-the-ramp sampling.

Items.Authors: Meryem Kubra Dag, Tolga Güver, Kieran O'Brien, David Barr, Sofia Dimoudi, John Connolly, Thomas Davies, Deli Geng, James Gill-Fleming, F. Korhan Yelkenci
Items.Title: Machine learning applications for real-time photon detection in MKIDs
Items.Abstract: MKIDs (Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors) are advanced superconducting detectors that can perform  real-time photon detection by measuring the change in surface impedance caused by incoming photons in a  simple LC circuit. These detectors have important advantages such as minimum readout noise, sensitivity in the  UVOIR spectrum, and high time resolution. However, the generation of large amounts of data at the microsecond  scale poses a significant challenge in the analysis of the raw data. In this study, machine learning methods trained  using monochromatic or multiwavelength light are proposed for real-time photon detection to solve the problem. Initial analyses using various machine learning algorithms yield results in detecting photons by processing resonator data and  determining their arrival time and energy. In the future, we aim to use this approach with GPUs to process data  from larger resonator arrays in real-time.

Items.Authors: François Rigaut, David Brodrick, Richard McDermid, Jennifer Burgess, Giovanni Cresci, Trevor Mendel, Simon Ellis, Anthony Horton, Scott Smedley, Maria Bergomi, Valentina Viotto, Roger Haynes, Pierre Haguenauer, Stefan Stroebele, Luca Marafatto, Bernardo Salasnich, Davide Greggio, Jesse Cranney, Antony Galla, Brian Taylor, Guido Agapito, Gaston Gausachs, Dionne Haynes, Enrico Pinna, Julien Bernard, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Elia Costa, Benoit Neichel, Tristan Monnier, Annino Vaccarella, Marco Gullieuszik, Timothy Chin, Nuria Lorente, Nuwanthika Fernando, Ross Zhelem, Cedric Plantet, Summer Luo, Marco Bonaglia, Matteo Aliverti, Mirko Colapietro, Kalyan Radhakrishnan, Simonetta Chinellato, Salvatore Savarese, Andrea Bianco, Rosanna Sordo, Daniela Fantinel, Max Hewlett, Lew Waller, Helen McGregor, Daniele Vassallo, Israel Vaughn
Items.Title: MAVIS: status after the final design review
Items.Abstract: MAVIS, the MCAO-Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph built by Astralis (Australia), INAF (Italy), LAM (France) and ESO, has passed Final Design Review in October 2025. The team is currently wrapping up action items following the review. We present the FDR system design, the expected performance, the procurement and the MAIT plans for this complex instrument. A MAVIS Science update is given elsewhere in this conference.

Items.Authors: Simonetta Chinellato, Mina Sibalic, Rosanna Sordo, Matteo Aliverti, Nicolò Azzaroli, Louis Barbier, Marco Bonaglia, Manal Chebbo, Christian Eredia, Paolo Ciliegi, Andrea Di Rocco, Laurent Jocou, Tommaso Lapucci, Marco Riva, Alfio Puglisi, Sylvain Rochat, Ludovico Teodori, Marco Xompero
Items.Title: MORFEO @ELT: where does RAM analysis lead to in design phase?
Items.Abstract: MORFEO (Multi-conjugate adaptive Optics Relay For ELT Observations) is the post-focal adaptive optics module for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope. The instrument provides MCAO correction for two instruments: MICADO and HARMONI.   Within the design of a complex Instrument as MORFEO, a Reliability, Availability and Maintainability (RAM) analysis needs to be addressed to increase the likelihood of success of the operations. Approaching FDR, the design needs a well identified RAM, as this is a design driver analysis that highlights criticalities for reliability aspects and allows the implementation of improvements that increase the availability of the instrument during the observations.   We will present how the major outcomes of the RAM analysis impacted the whole system requiring implementations in the design, via trade-offs that have been reached to comply to the requirements, especially when the preventive maintenance strategy was not sufficient to limit the risk of unavailability.

Items.Authors: Kirpal Nandra
Items.Title: The New Athena Wide Field Imager
Items.Abstract: The Wide-Field Imager (WFI) is one of two instruments aboard NewAthena, ESA’s future flagship X-ray observatory. It operates in the 0.2-15 keV range and with a 40x40 arcmin field of view is designed primarily to perform X-ray surveys and extended source observations.   The WFI consists of a large-format DEPFET active pixel sensor array, together with a smaller Fast Detector for high count rate applications. The DEPFETs deliver excellent energy resolution with high quantum efficiency and fast readout. They are controlled and read out by custom ASICs, with the resulting signals passed on to the Detector Electronics Subsystem, and then to the Instrument Control Subsystem, which interfaces with the spacecraft. The Primary Structure Subsystem provides the mechanical structure, and also houses the filter wheel.   In this presentation, the WFI status will be reviewed, in the light of the design and development progress which has been achieved during the NewAthena reformulation phase.

Items.Authors: Gong-Bo Zhao, Xiangqun Cui, Gang Zhao, Hua Bai, Heng Zuo, Kai Zhang, Xuefei Gong, Jiaru Chu
Items.Title: An Extremely Large Spectroscopic Survey Telescope (ESST) for astrophysical frontiers
Items.Abstract: The Extremely large Spectroscopic Survey Telescope (ESST) is a 12-metre spectroscopic survey facility featuring dual focal configurations: a Nasmyth focus with a 2-degree field of view, equipped with approximately 30,000–40,000 optical fibers; and a coudé focus integrated with ground-layer adaptive optics (GLAO), optimized for integrated field unit (IFU) observations of extended sources. ESST is expected to conduct a deep survey of galaxies and quasars, delivering an ideal sample that balances cosmic volume coverage and galactic mass completeness. Additionally, the telescope will acquire a statistically comprehensive sample encompassing hundreds of millions of stars across diverse stellar types, which will significantly advance our fundamental understanding of the Milky Way’s structure, formation, and evolution. As one of the top five major science facilities identified in China’s 2035 Development Strategy, ESST holds profound strategic significance for national astronomical research.

Items.Authors: Taro Shimizu, Jens Kammerer, Guillaume Bourdarot, Frank Eisenhauer, Julien Woillez, Jean-Baptiste Le Bouquin, Thibaut Paumard, Christian Straubmeier, Paulo Garcia, Sebastian Hoenig, Wolfgang Brandner, Laura Kreidberg, Frederic Gonte, Sylvain Oberti, Johann Kolb, Stefan Gillessen, Thomas Ott, Yixian Cao
Items.Title: First results from commissioning of the GRAVITY+ Adaptive Optics and Laser Guide Star systems at the VLTI
Items.Abstract: The GRAVITY+ project delivered in 2024 and 2025 four new sets of wavefront sensors and three new laser guide star systems to the VLTI. Together with the GRAVITY-Wide upgrade, this will revolutionize interferometry by providing significant improvements in sensitivity, sky coverage, and contrast. Here, we present the on-sky testing and commissioning of the new Natural Guide Star and Laser Guide Star modes with the GRAVITY instrument including updated performance metrics and the first science results. Fringe tracking on stars as faint as K=12.5 and deep integrations down to K=22 are now achievable enabling high redshift quasar observations out to z=4, the discovery of new exoplanets, extragalactic stellar interferometry, and resolving the structure of embedded YSOs.

Items.Authors: Simone Doniselli, Matteo Aliverti, Enrico Pinna
Items.Title: MAVIS: a flexure-based tip-tilt tool for arcsecond-level bonding of the pick-off mirrors
Items.Abstract: A dedicated tip–tilt gluing tool has been developed to meet the stringent angular alignment requirements of the pick-off mirrors in the MAVIS NGS Wavefront Sensor. Based on a compliant mechanism, the tool provides high stability, backlash-free motion, and sub-arcminute control, enabling pure rotational adjustment without lateral shifts. This significantly simplifies the bonding process and ensures reliable, repeatable positioning of the mirrors. A prototype has been built and its performance assessed, demonstrating its suitability for the tight tolerances of the MAVIS optical path.

Items.Authors: Jessica R. Lu, Antonin Bouchez, Brianna Peck, Rich Dekany, Peter Wizinowich, Renata Kupke, Prince Javier, Lianqi Wang, Kodi Rider, Brooke DiGia, Phil Hinz, Eduardo Marin
Items.Title: The Path to KOLA: A Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics System for Keck
Items.Abstract: We present progress on a conceptual design for a new Keck multi-conjugate adaptive optics (AO) system, called KOLA, capable of visible light correction with a near-diffraction-limited spatial resolution. The system will utilize a new adaptive secondary mirror (ASM), 2 high-altitude deformable mirrors (DMs), and ~8 laser guide stars (LGS). The field of regard for selecting guide stars will be ~2’ and the corrected science field will be 60”. We will also describe the planned path to KOLA, with an initial phase, called STRATA, that deploys new facility-wide AO infrastructure including the ASM and a new side-launched expandable LGS system that enables many new AO modes. We will describe science cases, system requirements, and performance simulations for both KOLA and STRATA phases. We will also present results from trade studies for the actuator count on the ASM, the number and brightness of the LGS, and the number and altitudes of the high-altitude DMs.

Items.Authors: Mina Sibalic, Vincenzo De Caprio, Matteo Genoni, Roberto Cirami, Stefano Covino, Bruno Castilho, Igor Coretti, Walter Seifert, Julian Stürmer, Sandi Wilson
Items.Title: CUBES RAMS-centered engineering approach from component to system reliability & safety
Items.Abstract: CUBES is a forthcoming VLT instrument designed for high-efficiency ultraviolet spectroscopy within the 300-400 nm range. This study presents a comprehensive Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Safety (RAMS) analysis, developed to ensure that CUBES achieves the target availability. The assessment integrates Functional Analysis, Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis (FMECA), Reliability Block Diagrams (RBD), and Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) budget at the subsystem level. The system comprises fifteen subsystems at Level 1 of the Product Breakdown Structure (PBS). Each subsystem is further divided into assemblies, subassemblies, units, and components. In parallel, the Safety Analysis applies Hazard Analysis and Fault Tree Analysis to identify, classify, and mitigate risks. The combined findings provide the identification of critical components and the development of preventive maintenance and operational risk-mitigation strategies for the CUBES Instrument.

Items.Authors: Paula Sanchez Saez, Claudio Reinero, Miguel Vioque, Markus Wittkowski, Marina Rejkuba, Martino Romaniello, Ashley Barnes, John Pritchard, Michaël Marsset
Items.Title: ESOFinder: an LLM-powered tool to help users navigate ESO documentation
Items.Abstract: The large volume and diversity of the European Southern Observatory (ESO) documentation —spanning the full observing lifecycle— make it difficult for astronomers to quickly find relevant information. To address this, we developed ESOFinder, a chatbot powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It integrates public information from manuals, Phase 1/2/3 docs, pipeline guides, the ESO Knowledge Base, and key web resources to deliver concise, context-aware, reference-linked answers on proposal preparation, observations, data retrieval, and processing. Built on open-source LLMs running on a local server, it ensures data privacy and full control of the knowledge base. ESOFinder is currently being tested internally to evaluate performance, workflow integration, and coverage. These tests guide improvements toward a reliable interface to navigate ESO’s complex documentation ecosystem and to support both staff and community astronomers in their daily tasks.

Items.Authors: André Fehlmann, D. Christopher Berst, Bret Goodrich, Isabelle F. Scholl, Erik Starman, Richard Summers, Armando Fajardo, Stuart Farrell, Dino Mensa, Matthew J. Reason
Items.Title: New digital infrared detectors for fast DKIST solar observations
Items.Abstract: The National Science Foundation Daniel K Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) has purchased multiple 4k x 4k, short-wavelength infrared focal plane modules (HgCdTe detector on a Silicon substrate) from Raytheon Vision Systems to replace the existing analog Hawaii 2RG devices currently used by the DL-NIRSP and Cryo-NIRSP instruments.     These new sensors meet our requirement of short global shutter exposures and fast full frame rates (60 Hz), which makes them ideally suited for high-flux solar disk observations. The capability of achieving long exposure times via non-destructive reads expands the use cases to high dynamic range scenes at the solar limb and the faint solar corona.  We will present the key performance metrics established for our new infrared cameras during acceptance testing and show their fundamental impact on our high-flux and high-dynamic-range solar observations.

Items.Authors: Vishambhar Nath Pandey, Bram Veenboer, Wilco Baan Hofman, Julian Kootstra, Jason Hessels, Ziggy Pleunis, Steven van der Vlugt, Jan David Mol
Items.Title: Scalable HPC cluster design for radio telescope front end and astronomical data processing
Items.Abstract: Modern radio telescopes and other data-intensive instruments require scalable, energy-efficient HPC infrastructures to support real-time signal processing and data intensive pipelines. We present a design approach for next-generation HPC clusters applicable from real-time front-ends to large-scale offline analytics. Drawing on experience from production systems - including GPU correlator/beamformer subsystems for LOFAR, the EuroFlash cluster with its integrated GPU beamformer, high-throughput BeeGFS-based storage architecture, and CPU-based production system - we outline key design patterns and lessons learned. We discuss architectural choices in heterogeneous computing, focusing on compute and I/O challenges such as CPU/accelerator balance, PCIe topology, and network design, along with low-latency high-throughput multi-petabyte storage systems. We address sustainability via performance, efficiency, and total cost of ownership showing how strategic choices lead to efficient solutions.

Items.Authors: David Polishook, Eran O. Ofek, Sagi Ben-Ami, Ofer Yaron, Alex Bichkovsky, Alexander Krassikchtchikova, Arie Blumenzweig, Enrico Segre, Michael Engel, Ofir Hershko, Omer Oreg, Oren Ironi, Ruslan Konno, Simone Garrappa, Yahel Sofer Rimlat
Items.Title: The new Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory (WAO)
Items.Abstract: The Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory is a new facility constructed and operated by the Weizmann Institute of Science (code M01; 35.041°E, 30.053°N; 400 m). The observatory focuses on arrays of small telescopes to demonstrate that such arrays can outperform a single seeing-limited large telescope of equal collecting area. The site will ultimately host 100 telescopes across two major arrays, the Large Array Survey Telescopes (LAST) and the Multi-Aperture Spectroscopic Telescope (MAST).

Items.Authors: Kristin K. Madsen, Andrew Ptak, Kimberly Banks, Simon Bandler, Barbara Grofic, Abe Falcone, Sven Herrmann, Steven Allen
Items.Title: The status of US NASA contributions to NewAthena
Items.Abstract: The ESA L-class mission, the Advanced Telescope for High Energy Astrophysics (Athena), was chosen for the Cosmic Vision program in 2014 to study the Hot and Energetic X-ray Universe. It was recently reformulated into NewAthena, a modified version of the original Athena. NASA has contributed to the technology and science since the early selection, and most recently, due to the redefinition, increased the scope of the contribution. The major hardware contribution is the kilo-pixel sensor for the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) and the readout circuits for it based on time-division multiplexing (TDM) with superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). NASA will also contribute the 4K cryocooler for the X-IFU and a vibration isolation system. AAdditional contributions include *support for* the Science Ground Segment *, design consultation* for the Wide Field Imager (WFI) *readout* ASIC and background analysis modeling for the WFI.

Items.Authors: Richard D. Stelter, Andrew Skemer, Steph Sallum, Nicholas K. Mac Donald, Renate Kupke, Christopher Ratliff, Ravinder Banyal, Thirupati Sivarani, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Emily Plume, Marc Kassis, Olivier Abseil, Natasha Batalha, Marc-Andre Boucher, Cyril Bourgenot, Will Deich, Devika Divakar, Michael Gonzales, Thomas Greene, Amirul Hasan, Phil Hinz, Becky Jensen-Clem, Chris Johnson, Govinda K. V., Isabel J. Kain, Mackenzie Lach, Jean-Thomas Landry, Jim Lyke, Ken Magone, Eduardo Marin, Rosalie McGurk, Raquel M. Martinez, Dimitri Mawet, Dale Sandford, Ramya Sethuam, Arun Surya, Eric Wang, Peyton Benac
Items.Title: Update on SCALES: the slicer combined with array of lenslets for exoplanet spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We give an update on the status of the thermal infrared (2-5 micron) low- to mid-spectral resolution (R=lambda/delta_lambda~20-5,000), lenslet-based, integral-field spectrograph and 1-5 micron imager, the Slicer Combined with Array of Lenslets for Exoplanet Science (SCALES). SCALES is deployed at the W. M. Keck Observatory behind the Keck II telescope’s Adaptive Optics (AO) system, and delivers diffraction-limited performance across its bandpass. The instrument has several key design features, including a selectable-wavelength monochromator for wavelength calibration; homologous construction of its bench, mechanisms, mounts, and optics; a slicer reimager to provide a discontinuous pseudoslit for mid-resolution spectroscopy; and a large, static lenslet array with two sub-arrays of lenslets used to feed a common spectrograph for both low- and mid-resolution modes. Since the 2024 SPIE meeting, SCALES has been fully integrated at UCSC and is expected to achieve first light in Spring 2026.

Items.Authors: Andreea Petric, Sarah Kendrew, Alberto Noriega-Crespo, Bryan Holler, Jane Morrison, Jonathan Aguillar, Stacey Alberts, Dean Hines, Greg Sloan
Items.Title: Wide field slitless spectroscopy with JWST's MIRI
Items.Abstract: Massively multiplexed spectroscopy enables efficient, statistically robust surveys of large cosmic volumes. Space-based wide-field slitless spectroscopy reduces cosmic variance by covering extensive sky areas with consistent sensitivity and calibration. In Cycle 5, JWST introduced a new MIRI prime observing mode—Wide Field Slitless Spectroscopy (WFSS)—which utilizes the P750L double prism to deliver low-resolution (R ~ 100) spectroscopy from 5 to 14 μm across an unobstructed 74″ × 113″ field of view. We present the MIRI WFSS calibration plans and their expected accuracy. We utilized established slitless-spectroscopy techniques from HST and JWST, archival P750L and MIRI imaging data, and dedicated calibration observations for flux/trace and wavelength calibration, including adjustments for positional dependencies. We present the most recent calibration reference files used for flat-fielding, background subtraction, and flux and wavelength calibration, and outline improvement plans.

Items.Authors: Aafaque R. Khan, William Verts, Harrison Bradley, Nazende Kerkeser, Daniel Turong, Elijah Garcia, Heejoo Choi, Haeun Chung, Daewook Kim, Carlos Vargas, Erika Hamden, Dave Hamara, Hannah Tanquary, Tom McMahon
Items.Title: Precision optical alignment of the Aspera far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrographs using computer-generated hologram (CGH) interferometry and vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) techniques
Items.Abstract: Aspera is a NASA SmallSat carrying two far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrographs to detect O VI emission near 1032 Å from the circumgalactic medium. The payload has a compact opto-mechanical layout and requires tight alignment tolerances and stringent contamination-control procedures. We report a multiphase optical alignment approach using computer-generated hologram (CGH) interferometry and FUV vacuum alignment. Reflective optics and gratings were aligned with a Zygo Fizeau interferometer and custom CGH in a class-1000 cleanroom under nitrogen purge. The two slits were aligned confocal with the off-axis parabola focus using a microscope system referenced to the Zygo laser spot, and the spacecraft star tracker was aligned to the instrument boresight with a 3D scanner. Final detector alignment and focus were performed in a vacuum VUV facility using a collimator, monochromator, and hollow-cathode flow lamp. The alignment is complete, and the instrument in preparation for launch in 2026.

Items.Authors: Florentin Millour, Bruno Lopez, Romain Petrov, Anthony Soulain, Philippe Bério, Alexis Matter, James Leftley, Julien Woillez, Jens Kammerer, Sylvestre Lacour, Jean-Baptiste Lebouquin, Walter Jaffe, Stéphane Lagarde, The MATISSE Team
Items.Title: MATISSE in the Laser Guide Stars Era: updated performance with the new GPAO adaptive optics, its LGS, and a new version of its DRS
Items.Abstract: We provide an overview of MATISSE at the VLTI in the context of GRAVITY+, following its performance update following the installation of GPAO in 2024 and LGS in 2025. We summarize the key instrumental features and observing modes, global data-reduction options, the new ergonomics of the user-friendly DRS, measurable quantities, and performance. MATISSE can be operated alone or with the GRAVITY fringe tracker in the so-called GRA4MAT mode. We present the updated MATISSE performance with GRA4MAT. When using the UTs, the added capabilities of GPAO and LGS are boosting the performance.

Items.Authors: Philippe Peille, Christophe Daniel, Vincent Albouys, Didier Barret, Aurora Simionescu, Luigi Piro, Massimo Cappi
Items.Title: Technical status of the X-ray Integral Field Unit before mission adoption
Items.Abstract: The X-ray Integral field Unit is an X-ray microcalorimeter, planned to be launched on the newAthena mission. With a cryostat passively cooled to 50 K, the heart of the instrument is organized within a 4K Core. This ensemble, cooled by a remote cryocooler, contains the Focal Plane Assembly (FPA) and the Multi-stage ADR (MAX), which provides the 50 mK cooling required by the detectors.   Approaching mission adoption, the architecture is being consolidated. In this contribution, we give an overview of the instrument technical status, emphasizing the main trade-offs that were conducted. This is followed by a summary of the demonstration activities performed at system level, focusing on the role of the 4K Core DM. This model will integrate demonstration versions of the FPA, MAX, but also of the cold harness. The cold detection chain, populated at the level of 1/4th of the flight model, will be read out by a set of demonstration models of the Warm Front-End and Digital Readout Electronics.
